BEING HUMAN (Section D: Moral Decision-making, Chapter 1)

OPENING QUOTE
- "The glory of God is the person fully alive." (St Irenaeus)
- The chapter's big idea: good and evil are part of human life, and being moral is part of our human nature.

THE EXISTENCE OF EVIL
- The chapter opens with an extract from Fergal Keane's book "Letter to Daniel: Despatches from the Heart".
- Fergal Keane is a journalist. He describes visiting Nyarubuye in Rwanda in early June, during the genocide of the Tutsis in Rwanda (1994).
- People in the account: Moses (the driver), Frank (a Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF) soldier acting as guide), Glenn (filming with the camera), Tony (the sound recordist), Valence (another guide, a boy), and David Harrison (team leader, a BBC producer with long experience of Africa).
- What they found: a red sandstone church. Above the door was a white marble statue of Christ with hands outstretched, and a banner celebrating Easter. Below it lay the body of a man across the steps.
- Bodies everywhere: a child who had been decapitated, a woman in a red cardigan and blue dress with a gash in her head, a child hacked almost in two, and a group of perhaps a hundred corpses - young and old, men and women - crowded at the door of the church offices. They had fled there as a group and were an easy target for machetes and grenades.
- The smell was "unlike anything I have ever experienced". It stayed with Keane for weeks afterwards.
- Keane began to pray the "Our Father", prayers he had not said since childhood, because he needed them now.
- Tony had tears in his eyes. Glenn kept stopping to cough. Keane stayed close to David Harrison because he needed his "age and strength and wisdom".
- Keane felt that journalism was "at best, a limited vehicle of expression, at worst a crude and inadequate tool" for showing evil "felt as a physical presence".
- He describes a fourteen-year-old boy who beat his elderly neighbour to death with a club and, cheered on by soldiers, killed other neighbours who were lying tied up on the ground.
- Keane borrows a phrase from the poet Yeats: a "pity beyond all telling".
- A detail from a memorial in Butare, Rwanda, remembers the victims of the genocide of April 1994.
- The textbook says "a pity beyond all telling" could also be said of:
- the attacks of 11 September 2001 in New York;
- Omagh on 16 August 1998;
- countless other mindless, forgotten atrocities.
- Most people agree that 11 September and Omagh were wrong and evil. The genocide in Rwanda is hard for us to think about because we have no pictures and it happened in a poor country in Africa - but it is the same evil.
- Questions the textbook raises: Why do people do something so evil? Can fear or revenge explain or justify such acts?

THE EXISTENCE OF GOOD
- Despite evil, there is great goodness in people.
- Aid organisations named: Trócaire, Concern, Gorta, Goal, Catholic Aid, Amnesty International, Society of St Vincent de Paul, Simon Community, L'Arche Community, The Red Cross, The Red Crescent.
- Every culture has produced people who work tirelessly for the good of humanity, who work for peace (often at risk to their own lives) and who give time and talents to the poor. Most are unknown.
- Why do people act like this? Three reasons given:
- because they know it is the right thing to do;
- because of their sense of justice;
- because they are following God's law of love for neighbour.
- Nobel Peace Prize winners 1993-2004 (listed in an assignment): Wangari Maathai (2004); Shirin Ebadi (2003); Jimmy Carter (2002); Kofi Annan and the United Nations (2001); Kim Dae-jung (2000); Médecins Sans Frontières (1999); John Hume and David Trimble (1998); Jody Williams and the International Campaign to Ban Landmines (1997); Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo and José Ramos-Horta (1996); Joseph Rotblat and the Pugwash Conferences (1995); Yasser Arafat, Shimon Peres and Yitzhak Rabin (1994); Nelson Mandela and F.W. de Klerk (1993).
- David Trimble and John Hume are pictured at the award ceremony in Oslo (1998).

LOOKING BEHIND GOOD AND EVIL
- The study of morality investigates good and evil: what makes one action right and another wrong?
- Sometimes it is easy to know the right thing to do; sometimes it is much harder.
- Morality is more than analysing actions: it is about the TYPE OF PEOPLE THAT WE ARE. What makes a person good or evil? What shapes how we think and the decisions we make?
- Three aspects of morality the course will look at:
- Our own experience: where does our own sense of good and evil come from?
- History: have peoples, writers and cultures through the ages agreed on what is good and evil?
- Religion: how do the different faiths influence our sense of good and evil?
- The starting point is our COMMON HUMANITY. Morality is a natural human phenomenon. People in general are moral.
- We look at how the human family tries to agree on what is good - to shape a "common moral canvas".

MORAL PRINCIPLES AND CODES OF BEHAVIOUR
- Principles: moral or ethical standards or judgements. Not everyone may agree with them, but they exist for particular reasons.
- Example school principles: all people must be treated with dignity; everyone has the right to an education.
- Principles may be summed up in a MISSION STATEMENT.
- Out of principles come RULES or CODES OF BEHAVIOUR. School examples:
- Principle: a school must provide a good educational environment. Rule: be in school by a certain time and stay until a certain time.
- Principle: everyone has a right to learn. Rule: classes should not be disrupted.
- Principle: all should be treated with dignity. Rule: everyone is treated with respect and not bullied.
- Key point: a code of behaviour arises out of a set of agreed principles.

KEY TERMS
- Morality: the study of good and evil and what makes an action right or wrong; being moral is part of human nature.
- Common humanity: the human nature we all share - the starting point for studying morality.
- Ethics: the study of human conduct, of how humanity understands good and evil, and how actions are judged right or wrong. It is a human discipline - part of who we are and common to all of us.
- Being moral: being a person who seeks to live a life of integrity according to a certain moral code.
- Christian ethics: the study of good and evil and right and wrong behaviour for those who believe in God and follow a Christian faith journey.
- Catholic moral theology: the study of good and evil and right and wrong behaviour in the Catholic Tradition.
- Universal global ethic: a broad, common statement of what humanity believes is right and wrong; a global consensus on good and evil.
- The Golden Rule: "Do to others as you would have them do to you." (Luke 6:31)

THE CATECHISM OF THE CATHOLIC CHURCH (CCC)
- Compiled and printed in English in 1994.
- A statement of the Catholic Church's teaching on faith and morality, in keeping with the spirit of the Second Vatican Council.
- Part Three is titled "Life in Christ" - this is where the Church's moral teaching is found.
- The text is divided into numbered paragraphs for ease of reference.

ONE MORALITY FOR ALL?
- Society has developed principles and codes about right and wrong. We do not always agree, but many are defined in state laws.
- Questions the course asks: Where do these principles come from? Who decides which apply? Can we all agree on good and evil? How does faith influence moral codes?
- Basic shared principles and codes:
- Principle: life should be protected. Code: the deliberate killing of a person is wrong.
- Principle: the right to own property. Code: theft is wrong.
- Society looks for consensus on shared principles at different levels:
- the international community at the United Nations;
- states (Ireland) or groups of states (European Union);
- religious communities (Catholic Church, Jewish community);
- the family unit, whose agreed principles shape each member's behaviour.
- Famous documents that express a community's principles:
- the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights (Eleanor Roosevelt is pictured holding it);
- the American Constitution: "We hold these truths to be self-evident...";
- the Ten Commandments (the Decalogue).
- The preamble to the UN Declaration proclaims it as "a common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations", to be promoted by teaching and education and secured by national and international measures.
- Actions showing a common human ethic: the trials in The Hague for war crimes in Bosnia in the early 1990s, and the Nuremberg trials after the Second World War. They show the international community asserting that a universal law governs all peoples.
- The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) is mentioned in an assignment.

A GLOBAL ETHIC
- Most people agree there is good and evil. Nearly everyone has a morality. Ethics crosses cultural and religious divisions.
- What is harder is agreeing on WHAT is right and wrong. Examples of disagreement:
- avoiding tax (some say it is their own money; others say it is immoral);
- using violence to change a corrupt government (some justify it; others say it is never right to kill);
- marriage to more than one woman (allowed in some cultures, immoral in others);
- abortion (illegal in some countries, a right in others).
- Cultures have had to decide on war, killing, marriage and divorce, justice for the poor, property rights and punishment - and have sometimes reached different conclusions.
- Some think there will always be a variety of moral beliefs because we come from different cultures and generations.
- Others believe we can agree a UNIVERSAL GLOBAL ETHIC.
- It cannot be for Westerners, Africans or Asians alone. Example: destroying the ozone layer or releasing a chemical weapon would be disastrous for all.
- It must be reached by CONSENSUS, through DIALOGUE. An ethic cannot be imposed; it must be agreed.
- International conferences on a global ethic: New Delhi, India (February 1993); Bangalore, India (August 1993); Chicago (September 1993), called the "Parliament of the World's Religions".
- Further reading: Hans Küng, "Global Responsibility: In Search of a New Ethic" (1991).

THE GOLDEN RULE
- One study found that a common morality could be grounded on the DIGNITY OF THE HUMAN PERSON: all people should be treated with dignity and allowed to live a life of dignity.
- Many see the Golden Rule as a good starting point. A form of it is found in many different traditions:
- Christianity: "Do to others as you would have them do to you." (Luke 6:31)
- Judaism: "What is hateful to you, do not do to others."
- Hinduism: "Do not do to others what would cause you pain if done to you."
- Buddhism: "Hurt not others in ways that you yourself would find hurtful."
- Islam: "No one of you is a believer until you desire for your sister or brother that which you desire for yourself."
- Taoism: "Regard your neighbour's gain as your own gain and your neighbour's loss as your own loss."
- The Golden Rule is part of morality "from Confucius to the philosopher Immanuel Kant".
- Maybe deep within all peoples, of any religion or none, there is a common morality.
- Example of applying it: "I would want people to tell me the truth no matter what, so I will tell the truth always to others."

THE COMMON STRUGGLE AGAINST EVIL
Crimes against humanity
- The term suggests some actions are inherently wrong and damage the whole of humanity.
- On 11 September 2001, President McAleese called the attacks an attack on the whole of humanity, not just on people in the United States.
- Wars continually happen. Some get lots of attention (Iraq); others very little (the Congo). Many acts of violence go unreported.
- If we see ourselves as a common humanity, these atrocities are crimes against all of us.
- Crimes against humanity are not only in war: absolute poverty, the exploitation of children, and the lack of resources for poor countries to fight the AIDS epidemic could also be seen as crimes against the human family.
- Prisons and punishment exist in every society - a sign of humanity's efforts at a universal system of justice. There is no agreed universal justice system, but there are growing efforts to call certain criminals to account anywhere in the world.
- Assignments mention: the genocide in Rwanda (Fergal Keane's "Season of Blood"); the ethnic cleansing of Muslim Bosnians; the genocide in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Corruption in public life
- Citizens, especially in democracies, want more accountability from public representatives - "ethics in public life".
- "Power corrupts, and absolute power corrupts absolutely." (Lord Acton)
- Irish tribunals investigating immoral and illegal actions by powerful people:
- Flood/Mahon Tribunal: planning matters in Dublin in the 1980s and 1990s.
- McCracken and Moriarty Tribunal: payments to politicians.
- Lindsay Tribunal: the Blood Transfusion Board's treatment procedures for haemophiliacs.
- Laffoy/Ryan Tribunal: child abuse in residential institutions run by religious orders on behalf of the State.

Identifying principles behind evil actions (textbook examples)
- Using children as soldiers is wrong because children are not free to choose and have a right to protection.
- A married person having an affair is wrong because it breaks a commitment, causes hurt to others and is living a lie.

SUMMARY
- Human beings, as individuals and communities, constantly struggle against evil and work to achieve good for others. Being moral is part of our human nature.
- Good and evil are part of life. The human family lives by guiding principles.
- It is difficult to reach a common ethic for all humanity, but some acts are universally seen as evil, and world society has tried to punish them.
- There are many examples - international, national and community - of the human family seeking good and punishing evil.

rows.prompt: State the Golden Rule and give its form in two other religions.
rows.model_answer: Christianity: 'Do to others as you would have them do to you' (Luke 6:31). Judaism: 'What is hateful to you, do not do to others.' Buddhism: 'Hurt not others in ways that you yourself would find hurtful.'

rows.prompt: What is a universal global ethic, and why must it be agreed rather than imposed?
rows.model_answer: It is a broad, common statement of what humanity believes is right and wrong - a global consensus on good and evil. It must come through dialogue and consensus because an ethic cannot be imposed on people; it has to be agreed by all.

rows.prompt: Name the four levels at which society seeks consensus on shared principles.
rows.model_answer: The international community at the United Nations; states like Ireland or groups like the European Union; religious communities like the Catholic Church or Jewish community; and the family unit.

rows.prompt: Explain in your own words what is meant by a 'crime against humanity', with an example.
rows.model_answer: It is an action that is wrong in itself and damages the whole human family, not just its direct victims. For example, President McAleese called the 11 September 2001 attacks an attack on all humanity. The chapter adds that absolute poverty and child exploitation could also be seen as crimes against our human family.

rows.prompt: Name two Irish tribunals and what each investigated.
rows.model_answer: The Flood/Mahon Tribunal investigated planning matters in Dublin in the 1980s and 1990s. The McCracken and Moriarty Tribunal investigated payments to politicians.

rows.prompt: Discuss the possibility of a universal global ethic. In your answer refer to the Golden Rule. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Most people agree that there is good and evil, and nearly everyone has a morality; ethics crosses cultural and religious divisions. The difficulty is agreeing on what is right and wrong. Cultures disagree about things such as avoiding tax, using violence against a corrupt government, marriage to more than one wife, and abortion. Some thinkers say that because we come from different cultures and generations there will always be a variety of moral beliefs. Others believe we can agree a universal global ethic: a broad common statement of what humanity believes is right and wrong. It cannot belong to one group, because problems such as destroying the ozone layer or using a chemical weapon affect everyone. It must be reached by consensus through dialogue, not imposed. Conferences in New Delhi, Bangalore and Chicago (the 'Parliament of the World's Religions') in 1993 tried to develop such an ethic. The Golden Rule suggests a shared foundation. Christianity says 'Do to others as you would have them do to you' (Luke 6:31); Judaism says 'What is hateful to you, do not do to others'; Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism and Taoism have similar forms, and it runs from Confucius to Kant. One study found a common morality could be grounded on the dignity of the human person. So, while full agreement is hard, a common morality may lie deep within all peoples.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: agreement that good and evil exist; examples of moral disagreement between cultures; meaning of a universal global ethic; consensus and dialogue, not imposition; ozone/chemical weapon example; 1993 conferences; Golden Rule in at least two traditions; dignity of the human person; Confucius to Kant.

rows.prompt: Explain the relationship between moral principles and codes of behaviour. Use examples from school life and from society. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: Principles are moral or ethical standards or judgements. Codes of behaviour, or rules, come out of these principles, so a code of behaviour arises out of a set of agreed principles. In a school, the principle that everyone has a right to learn leads to the rule that classes should not be disrupted. The principle that all should be treated with dignity leads to the rule that no one is bullied. A school might sum up its principles in a mission statement. Society works the same way. The principle that life should be protected leads to the code that deliberate killing is wrong, and the principle of the right to own property leads to the code that theft is wrong. Many of these codes are written into state laws. Documents like the UN Declaration of Human Rights and the Ten Commandments express the principles of a community.
rows.marking_scheme: Definition of principle 2 marks; principle-to-code link explained 2 marks; school example 3 marks; society example 3 marks.

rows.prompt: 'Good and evil are part of life.' Discuss this statement with reference to examples given in the chapter. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: The chapter shows that evil is real. Fergal Keane described entering the church at Nyarubuye in Rwanda during the genocide of the Tutsis. Under a statue of Christ and an Easter banner lay bodies, including a child who had been decapitated and about a hundred people killed by machetes and grenades at the church office door. He described evil 'felt as a physical presence', and a fourteen-year-old boy who killed his neighbours, cheered on by soldiers. He called it, in Yeats' words, 'a pity beyond all telling'. The same could be said of 11 September 2001 and Omagh on 16 August 1998. Yet there is also great goodness. Organisations like Trócaire, Concern, Goal, the Simon Community and the Red Cross work for others. Every culture has people who work for peace, often at risk to their lives, and who give their time to the poor. They act because it is right, from a sense of justice, or because they follow God's law of love for neighbour. Nobel Peace Prize winners such as John Hume and David Trimble show this. The human family also fights evil through tribunals, war crimes trials at The Hague and Nuremberg, and prisons. So being moral, and struggling against evil, is part of our human nature.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: Keane in Rwanda (details); Yeats' phrase; 11 September and Omagh; aid organisations; reasons people do good; Nobel Peace Prize winners; trials and tribunals; being moral is part of human nature.

rows.prompt: Outline how the human family at international and national level struggles against evil. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: At international level, the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights sets 'a common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations'. The trials in The Hague for war crimes in Bosnia in the early 1990s, and the Nuremberg trials after the Second World War, show the international community asserting that a universal law governs all peoples. The idea of a 'crime against humanity' says some actions harm everyone; President McAleese called the 11 September attacks an attack on the whole of humanity. Absolute poverty, child exploitation and the lack of resources for poor countries to fight AIDS can also be seen as crimes against the human family. Prisons exist in every society, and there are growing efforts to call certain criminals to account anywhere in the world. At national level, citizens want ethics in public life, recalling Lord Acton's words that 'power corrupts, and absolute power corrupts absolutely'. Ireland set up tribunals: Flood/Mahon on planning in Dublin, McCracken and Moriarty on payments to politicians, Lindsay on the Blood Transfusion Board and haemophiliacs, and Laffoy/Ryan on child abuse in residential institutions. These show society holding powerful people to account.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: UN Declaration; Hague and Nuremberg trials; crimes against humanity; McAleese on 11 September; poverty/AIDS as crimes against humanity; prisons and universal justice; Lord Acton; named Irish tribunals and their subjects.

rows.prompt: Distinguish between ethics, Christian ethics and Catholic moral theology, and explain the role of the Catechism of the Catholic Church. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: Ethics is the study of human conduct, of how humanity understands good and evil, and how actions are judged right or wrong. It is a human discipline common to all people. Christian ethics is the same study for those who believe in God and follow a Christian faith journey. Catholic moral theology is the study of good and evil and right and wrong behaviour in the Catholic Tradition. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (CCC), printed in English in 1994, states the Church's teaching on faith and morality in the spirit of the Second Vatican Council. Its moral teaching is in Part Three, 'Life in Christ', and it is divided into numbered paragraphs for easy reference. So the three terms move from the general human study to the study within a particular faith tradition.
rows.marking_scheme: Ethics 3 marks; Christian ethics 2 marks; Catholic moral theology 2 marks; CCC (1994, Vatican II, Part Three 'Life in Christ') 3 marks.
